_about: Item 166: every tone and term has one definition. The single source of every legend, the glossary route and the client report's appendix. `word` is as drawn; `engine` is the payload or engine name it maps to; `full` is a paragraph whose first sentence is the in-place disclosure. `class` binds a tone to its stylesheet rule. `matches` lists the exact strings a client report is searched for, so only terms that carry it can reach an appendix. One definition per word (item 263): an entry with `same_as` is the same word drawn in another place. It keeps its own id, group, tone class and engine name, and takes its word and definition from the entry it names, so a legend or chip naming it still works and the glossary and a client report's appendix list the word once.

entries.full: A control that does something and costs nothing to press. It reads the stored record or runs a check that calls no paid model.
A control that does something and spends money on a model when pressed. Its label states the estimated cost before you press it, and it asks first, naming what runs, where and the price.
The one thing the screen suggests you do next. There is at most one on a screen, and none when nothing is next.

A control that does something and spends nothing, other than the screen's main action. It is outlined, so the one filled control on a screen stays the next step. It does what it says on the press, with no confirmation, because nothing it does costs money or cannot be put back.
A control whose result cannot be undone, such as deleting. It is marked by consequence, not by cost. It asks first, naming what goes and what depends on it.
Takes you somewhere else on the screen without changing anything. It never starts an action and never spends.
A fault that stops search engines or visitors reaching or trusting the page. Fix these before anything else.
A fault that measurably costs visibility or visitors. Fix these soon.
A fault worth fixing that is unlikely on its own to cost much. Fix these as part of normal work.
A small improvement. Fix these when the page is next edited.
Something worth knowing that is not a fault. Nothing needs to be done.
A fault the latest audit still found. It stays open until an audit no longer finds it.
A fault that was fixed and has come back. It counts as open, and it is marked so the return is not missed.
A fault an audit found and a later audit no longer finds. If it returns it becomes regressed.

A finding an analysis reported that nothing has confirmed yet. Where the automatic checks raise the same check in the same audit, it opens. Where they cannot, or have read the page twice since without raising it, it is "to confirm" and waits for you. If the analysis runs again, reads the page and no longer reports it, it is dropped rather than counted as fixed.
A finding taken back because it was wrong. It stays in the record so the correction is visible.

An automatic finding about a page that now answers an error, so the check no longer applies there. It leaves the open count. It is not a fix: if the page answers again and the check still fires, it reopens as open.
A fault you have chosen to live with. It stays in the record and no longer counts as open.
A finding whose pages the site no longer serves. It is kept for the record, but there is nothing left to fix.

Written by a model reading the evidence, not measured by a check. An analysis reads one part of the site at a time and writes what it judges worth fixing; each is priced before it runs, and it is not scored.
Found by an automatic check reading the pages, with no model involved. The automatic checks run in every audit, count every instance they can match, and cost nothing.
Cannot be judged until you supply an input, such as the site's stack or who may be probed. Admin holds the inputs.
Ranks above everything else, because nothing else matters until it is fixed. At most one thing is marked this way.
How many faults are open. A shaded number means there is something to do.
How many of something there are, with no judgement about whether that is good or bad.
A count of zero, drawn quietly so it does not compete with the counts that need attention.
Marks the place on the screen you are looking at now.
A fix made once in a shared page template that repairs every page built from it.
A fix made in the process that builds or publishes pages, not in any one page.
A fix that is a decision or a server setting rather than a change to page content.
The measured value is inside the range that block holds it to. The range is stated on the block's threshold line.
The measured value is close to or just past the range that block holds it to. It is worth watching, and it is not yet a fault on its own.
The measured value is outside the range that block holds it to. The block's findings say what to change.
A value shown for context, with no range to hold it to.
The pages this audit fetched. A count out of crawled pages says how common something is among the pages that were actually read.
The site as one subject rather than a set of pages. A count about the site is never shown as a share of pages.
Everything stored for this site across every audit, including pages the site no longer serves. It is bookkeeping, and nothing is divided by it.
A count shown with the group it was counted out of, because that group differs from what the heading covers. The words after it name the group.

This audit did not measure it, so it has no result either way: it neither passes nor fails, and it is neither good nor bad. The sentence beside it says why: the part has not run, the scope leaves it out, or the site record lacks what the check needs.
A check that ran but whose result is not shown, because a more specific check already reports the same fault. The because-clause names which.
The check has no meaning for this site, for example language alternates on a single-language site. It is not a pass.
Runs no paid model. Checks and stored readings are free.
Sends evidence to a paid language model, which writes a judgement. The cost is estimated before it runs.
One URL you name. Nothing is followed from it, so what the audit says is about that page alone.
The pages the site puts in its header and footer, its own claim about what matters. It is the smallest scan that still covers what a visitor is offered first.
A representative sample, capped. The cap is the one a Standard audit has always used, so two site scans of one site are comparable.
Every reachable page, nothing sampled out. It is the only scan whose coverage can reach 100%, and the longest to run.
A barrier in what every page shares, such as the header, navigation or footer. One edit there clears it on every page.
A barrier in the template one group of pages is built from. One edit clears it on that group.
A barrier in one page's own content. Each page is its own edit, which is why it is the long tail of the fix order.
The number of distinct websites that link to this one, as a backlink provider counts them. It is recorded for reference: a provider's count, not a crawl of the web.
A backlink provider's own 0 to 100 score for a site. It is a third-party proxy, so it is shown for reference and affects no score here.
How the visible text of the links pointing at a site is spread across phrases. One phrase making up most of it reads as unnatural; the provider supplies it or it is not measured.
Name, address and phone number: the three facts a local listing must state the same way everywhere it appears. A mismatch between the site and a listing is a NAP inconsistency.
A mention of the business's name, address and phone on another website, such as a directory or a map listing. Citations agreeing with the site is what makes them count.

An analysis looked and could not judge this check here, and its reason says what it would need. It is a hold, not a result: it neither passes nor fails, and it differs from not measured, which is a check this audit did not run.
Applies a fixed checklist. No model judgement. It is free, and the honest first pass on a large site: a checklist over every page beats judgement over a sample when the fault is template-level.
Analysis with judgement at the edges. A model reads what the checks leave open. The page budget is the scope's, not this choice's.
Where the judgement is the product. It is the fullest reading of the evidence the scope gathered, and the most expensive; what it reads is still the scope's page set.
Every part of the site with something open, most important first. Each row opens that part.
How much of the site the audits have actually looked at, and what they could not measure. A zero where nothing looked is not a zero where nothing is wrong.
What is fixed, accepted or withdrawn, and what changed since the last audit.
This has not run on this site before, so there is no measured price to show. It still spends when it runs, and that first run is what gives it a price.
The price of this, for what is selected now, has not been read yet. The control is held until it has, so nothing is spent against a price that was never on screen.
Once confirmed, what this removes is gone and there is no undo. Anything that read it stops having it, and the confirmation names what that is.
The site has been audited again since this report was written, so it may name findings a later audit has closed. Counted over full readings of the site: a re-check of one part does not age it.

The client report cannot go out for this audit yet, because some of its Critical or High findings have not been assessed. Mark each one fixed, accepted risk or withdrawn, from the record, and the hold lifts on every screen at once.

A row recording something this audit could not measure - a check whose provider is unconfigured, a page the crawl never fetched. It is not a finding, is never counted with them, and cannot be assessed: there is nothing to decide. Screens that state a findings count state how many notes they set aside.

Every address this audit actually requested. It is a list of what was fetched, so two addresses that differ only by a query string are two entries - and that is worth seeing, because it is the site serving one page under two spellings.

The pages an audit measured, counted once each: the addresses it fetched with the query string stripped. Every count on a client screen is over this, never over the fetched list, because a page counted twice would make a fault look twice as common.

Something the operator wrote about a client, kept with the site. Nothing to do with a coverage note, which is the engine saying what it could not measure - the two shared the word "note" in the bar and the headline until 2026-09-18.
A check ran on this scope and found nothing to fix. It is the only one of the three states that is a clean result, and it is said only where something was measured.

The check does not fire on this scope by construction, so nothing here is neither a pass nor a gap. A site with one locale has no hreflang to get wrong; a page with no JSON-LD has no markup to validate.
The screen's one main action, filled. There is at most one on a screen, and none when nothing is next.
Changes here save as soon as you pick them. Each row says when it saved, or why it did not.
Nothing here is saved until you press save. Leaving the screen first keeps nothing you typed.
Runs a part's automatic checks again, for free, and replaces what they found. It is the one word for that action on every part; an analysis a model writes is run, not re-checked.
Opens an analysis finding that waits for you, as a fault the site has. It then counts like any open finding, including toward the report hold.
Keeps a finding on the record as a known risk you have chosen to live with. It stops counting as open and is never reopened automatically.
Retracts a finding as never true. It is not a repair and nothing gets credit for one. An audit that sees the fault again puts it back.
No analysis has read this part against the audit you are looking at. A part read on an earlier audit says how many audits ago, because the site has moved since.

Measured longer ago than the age you set in Admin, 90 days unless changed. The page may have changed since; re-check the part to measure it again. From a shorter age, 30 days unless changed, a date says it may be out of date.
Marks a part in the parts strip whose automatic checks were last measured longer ago than the out-of-date age. Re-check the part to measure it again.

The answer for what you have chosen has not arrived yet. Until it does the screen draws no count, no empty state and no sentence from an earlier choice, because a figure shown while it is still being read would be read as true.
Read by a check or a model in this audit. Something not assessed has no result either way.
The share of the site's pages an audit read. Findings speak only for the pages covered.
Open and regressed findings together: everything still to do.

An analysis finding nothing automatic will ever confirm: its check is one only a model can raise, or the automatic checks have read the page twice since without raising it. A second run of the same model is not confirmation, so it stays out of the report hold and the client report until you Confirm, Accept or Withdraw it.
A site score of 80 or above out of 100.
A site score of 60 to 79 out of 100.
A site score below 60 out of 100.
No audit has completed on this site, so it has no score. It is a state, not missing data.
One pass of the product over the site: a crawl, the automatic checks, and any analyses chosen. Where the screen says audit, the engine records a run.
Largest Contentful Paint is how long the biggest visible element takes to appear. Google uses it as one of its Core Web Vitals, and Search Console and PageSpeed report it under the same name.
Cumulative Layout Shift is how much the page moves around while it loads. It is a Core Web Vital, and lower is better.
Interaction to Next Paint is how quickly the page responds when someone taps or clicks. It is a Core Web Vital and can only be measured from real visitors.
Time to First Byte is how long the server takes to start answering. A slow start delays everything after it.
Total Blocking Time is how long scripts keep the page from responding while it loads. It is a laboratory stand-in for INP.
The canonical is the address a page names as its preferred version. Search engines use it to choose one address when several show the same content.
Hreflang is markup that tells search engines which language or country version of a page to show. Each version must name the others and itself.
The robots.txt file at the root of the site tells crawlers which addresses they may fetch. It controls crawling, not whether a page is indexed.
JSON-LD is the format Google recommends for structured data. It describes what a page is about, such as a business, a product or an article, in a form machines read.
A sitemap is a file listing the addresses a site wants search engines to find. Listing a page does not guarantee it is indexed.
Noindex is an instruction on a page telling search engines not to show it in results. A page carrying it by mistake disappears from search.
Schema.org is the shared vocabulary of types, such as Organization, Product and LocalBusiness, that structured data is written in.
The site's robots.txt tells this crawler it is blocked. Someone decided this, and the file says so.
The firewall refuses this crawler, and the site record declares that refusal deliberate. Robots.txt does not say so, but the operator has.
The firewall turned this crawler away with nothing said in robots.txt and nothing declared on the site record. Nobody decided this, so it is the one to look at.
This audit visited as the crawler and was let in and shown the page. It says the firewall answered that crawler name, not what the crawler then did.
Robots.txt says nothing to this crawler and there is nothing to visit. It applies to robots tokens such as Google-Extended, which are settings rather than visitors.
This audit did not visit as this crawler, so nothing is claimed either way. It is never shown as a pass.
A crawler that collects pages to build training sets. Blocking it changes nothing you can see in any AI answer.
A crawler its vendor uses to improve its own models. Blocking it is a choice about your content, with nothing visible in any answer.
A crawler that builds an answer engine's own search index ahead of time. Blocking it removes the site from that engine's results and citations.
A crawler that fetches a page when someone asks an assistant a question. Blocking it means the assistant could not look.

A figure our own browser measured, on one load of one page, not a figure from your visitors. The load runs on a throttled mid-tier phone and 4G profile so two audits can be compared, and that profile is stated above the pictures.

A figure taken from real visits to the site, as Google's public record of them reports it. It covers the slowest quarter of those visits over the reporting window, and exists only for a URL with enough traffic for Google to publish one, so a small site can have none.
A title or description wider than the cut at the viewport its check measures. The part past the cut is what a result leaves off; the strip draws the cut as a dashed line.
A title or description within the cut and at or above the minimum length. Nothing about its length is raised.
A title or description under the minimum number of characters. Google may write its own in its place.
No title or no description on the page at all. The strip draws it hatched at a fixed height, so it is not read as a short value.

The phone screen a cut-off length is measured against. A result is given less room on a phone than on a desktop, so a title can be cut on one and whole on the other. The width is on the line beside the word: 410 px for a title.

The desktop screen a cut-off length is measured against. The width is on the line beside the word and differs by field: 600 px for a title, 920 px for a description, which is only ever measured on desktop.
